messages.author: ea8ef9b751c1cafe
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
parts:
I did some work implementing CVODE as an ODE solver in Stan. CVODE is a really great solver, the implementation has been around for many years and based on even older fortran code.
It can deal with stiff ODEs and with failure cases when there are instabilities.

I'm collaborating with statisticians in Pharma as well as academics with lots of ODE models that don't fit in the box of nice models that RK45 can deal with. Most of the work up till now has been using custom build software, but I also would like to contribute the knowledge gained with the wonderful effort of Stan.

Unfortunately, CVODE is obviously a little bit more heavy for simpler models such as the harmonic oscillator or Lorenz. But there is definitely a gain with more complex models as it can deal with stiff models and usually take large time steps. I'm now trying to get the authorization from my collaborators to release some of the models and the data that we are working with to the Stan community. Those definitely require a more advanced solver.

I'm also working on an implementation of a more advanced technique to compute the gradients: there are cases when the sensitivity approach is too expensive. But this might take a little while longer to complete.

Would you be interested in this work or discussing it further?

As for lsoda/cvoda, both solvers are based on the same algorithms (BDF or Adams-Moulton). Both have also been around for a long long time and started out as Fortran code. I believe CVODE is a reimplementation (also geared towards parallelism) whereas lsoda is an automatic translation to C.
They are basically the de-facto standard for any ODE solving (except for the easy cases). I have a slight preference for CVODE, but I would say there is no real difference.
As for the jacobians, both packages can compute the jacobians using finite differencing but the user can also provide it as a function in dense or sparse format. I don't think that the Adams-Moulton algorithm uses Jacobians, since it's basically a Runge-Kutta + correction. For the sensitivity solution, the jacobian might involve higher-order derivation of the righ-hand side but FD might be fine. But there are different ways to go about this.

Tom

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
parts:
That would be a big "yes". We'd love to have help
adding stiff solvers to Stan. It's our highest
priority to-do item for new language features and also
the one with which we have the least experience.

We've been doing applied work on some PK/PD and
also some soil-carbon models based on ODEs and other
users have been asking us for stiff solvers.

We're particularly interested in sorting out finite diffs
vs. autodiff gradients. As you may have seen, we have built
a coupled system for the non-stiff case that lets us compute
the first-order gradients we need for Euclidean HMC and optimization.

Michael Betancourt worked out the math for the coupled system
with Jacobians we'd need for implementing our own Jacobians
using autodiff, but we're interested also in the finite diffs
built in if they're not too cumbersome. The problem is that
doing the Jacobians would require higher-order autodiff on the
coupled system, and we're just getting the kinks worked out
of higher-order autodiff and it hasn't been very highly optimized
yet. We're also working on alternative autodiff we plan to plug
in at some point.

Other people with ODE solver experience have echoed
your sentiments about CVODE (and Sundials in general) and lsoda.
It's great they both have compatible licenses.

What did you mean that CVODE is heavier for simpler
models? More memory or time? If it's just integration headache,
we have to take that on anyway.

- Bob

messages.author: ea8ef9b751c1cafe
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
parts:
We've been working on ODE problems exclusively for over a year now. Mostly focused on parallelism and performance aspects. So sounds like a great match :)
The parallelism bit is also something I would love to contribute, but that is probably something more long term.

I have a working prototype which needs some more optimizations and linking needs to be cleaned up. The current coupled system uses std::vector a lot which doesn't fit nicely with CVODE's C interface, so at the moment it does some extra copying which isn't really required. Additionally it uses CVODE's built-in FD to compute Jacobians, which might still needs to be replaced as it would make the method much more efficient. Without resorting to higher-order autodiff, applying FD outside of CVODE could be beneficial because of the structure of the jacobian. Since CVODE has no idea about this structure it needs to do tons of extra work. I'll look into this next week.

For the simple models such as the oscillator, a stiff solver (such as BDF) is just overkill and something like Runge-Kutta or Adams-Moulton is perfect. But this can easily be an options for the user. In the next two weeks, we are hopefully able to release some of the models + data.

Tom

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
parts:
Hey,

I've put my latest version on my github fork: https://github.com/tomhaber/stan/tree/cvode

I just added the code providing jacobians to CVODE as discussed previously: instead of CVODE doing finite differencing, this code does finite differencing internally for computing the hessians. It can exploit the structure of the jacobian to compute it much faster: should be in order of #parameters faster.
When/if higher-order autodiff becomes available, this internal finite differencing can then be easily replaced.

The simple unit tests seem to work, but I should run a test on my other models as well.

The linking would be something that you guys could definitely help with. I'm currently using an ugly hack to completely avoid it. The header-only thing makes it a little hard. When I briefly looked at it, I could only see a possibility of adding it into the R binding code.

For now, it is more of a prototype. I use a wrapper that I made to hide any ode solver, but it might not make sense now (Unless you consider other ode solvers at some point). The implementation can be cleaned up/simplified otherwise.

Tom

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
parts:
Hey Daniel,

What seems to be the problem with the installation? Should be as simple
as "make && make install".

My problem was just when to do the linking correctly according to stan
rules. I guess rstan should do it, but all other derived packages should
know about CVODE as well. I couldn't link it into the stan library
(which now also doesn't exist anymore it seems).

As a side-note, definitely not all ODEs are stiff and the real problem
might be in the model itself (but stan shouldn't silently fail here).
Runga-kutta 45 is a good solver for a lot of problems, but the
implementation in boost is just not stable. CVODE on the other hand is
tried and proven. If people worry about the cost of an implicit solver,
CVODE also includes an explicit one and it is possible for an implicit
solver to take huge steps and still outperform a simple explicit solver.
Just my 2 cents...

Regards,
Tom

On Fri, Apr 17, 2015 at 7:43 AM, Tom Haber <tom....@uhasselt.be> wrote:
Hey Daniel,

What seems to be the problem with the installation? Should be as simple
as "make && make install".

My problem was just when to do the linking correctly according to stan
rules. I guess rstan should do it, but all other derived packages should
know about CVODE as well. I couldn't link it into the stan library
(which now also doesn't exist anymore it seems).

As a side-note, definitely not all ODEs are stiff and the real problem
might be in the model itself (but stan shouldn't silently fail here).
Runga-kutta 45 is a good solver for a lot of problems, but the
implementation in boost is just not stable. CVODE on the other hand is
tried and proven. If people worry about the cost of an implicit solver,
CVODE also includes an explicit one and it is possible for an implicit
solver to take huge steps and still outperform a simple explicit solver.
Just my 2 cents...

Regards,
Tom

parts:
Had a chance to talk to Tom — we’ll spend plenty more time talking over
the next few days.  Firstly, the code in Tom’s repo should be up to date
with the current implementation.  What’s great is that CVODE could be
called from the C++ with a simple extern which bodes well for integration.
He also finite-differenced the autodiff gradients to approximate the Hessian
to compute the Jacobian instead of letting CVODE compute it implicitly.
It might be worth using the block-diagonal approximation to test integration
without having to wait for the higher-order autodiff.

There seem to be some stability issues but hopefully we can figure that
out when we work through the implementation.

Daniel

On Fri, Apr 17, 2015 at 7:43 AM, Tom Haber <tom....@uhasselt.be> wrote:
Hey Daniel,

What seems to be the problem with the installation? Should be as simple
as "make && make install".

My problem was just when to do the linking correctly according to stan
rules. I guess rstan should do it, but all other derived packages should
know about CVODE as well. I couldn't link it into the stan library
(which now also doesn't exist anymore it seems).

As a side-note, definitely not all ODEs are stiff and the real problem
might be in the model itself (but stan shouldn't silently fail here).
Runga-kutta 45 is a good solver for a lot of problems, but the
implementation in boost is just not stable. CVODE on the other hand is
tried and proven. If people worry about the cost of an implicit solver,
CVODE also includes an explicit one and it is possible for an implicit
solver to take huge steps and still outperform a simple explicit solver.
Just my 2 cents...

Regards,
Tom

I have questions, then things I think we should do before we get it into the code base.

Questions:
1) Is the branch on your fork the latest version?
2) Could we move that to the main repo (github.com/stan-dev/stan)? I'd be happy to give you permissions to the main repo (if you don't already).
3) Have you dealt with conditional builds? I haven't thought too much about it, but we definitely want Stan to build even without having installed CVODE.

Things we need to do:
1) tests: unit tests, tests to make sure all generated ODEs work
2) doc: at the class level, in the documentation
3) evaluations: how do the different solvers (within and outside of CVODE) compare. Does it actually do a reasonable job with a stiff solver on a non-stiff problem? Should we be looking at ARKode or LSODA instead?



Daniel

parts: On Thu, 2015-05-21 at 09:58 -0400, Daniel Lee wrote:

> I have questions, then things I think we should do before we get it
> into the code base.
>
>
> Questions:
>
> 1) Is the branch on your fork the latest version?
>
It is my latest/final version, but it is based on an older version of

stan/rstan. Since the big refactoring of the stan code, things seem to
have moved around quite a bit.

> 2) Could we move that to the main repo (github.com/stan-dev/stan)? I'd
> be happy to give you permissions to the main repo (if you don't
> already).
>

I could do that. I don't know how to deal with the dependence on an old
version of rstan however.

> 3) Have you dealt with conditional builds? I haven't thought too much
> about it, but we definitely want Stan to build even without having
> installed CVODE.
>

I have done this many times and it's easy to do. Not sure how to do it
in the stan build system however. If this is not available in the
current build system, I'm afraid you'll need to add this feature. I
usually work with autotools or cmake.
>
>

> Things we need to do:
>
> 1) tests: unit tests, tests to make sure all generated ODEs work
>

Since my implementation is a drop-in replacement for the existing
solver, I'm just using the existing unit tests. I did need to change
some of the thresholds as I'm asking for such an accurate solution from
CVODE that the tests fail because the FD gradients are not good as a
reference. This was all checked in matlab with the true analytic
solutions. Maybe it's a good idea to add this as a unit test as well,
using the true analytic solution as a reference instead of the FD
estimate.

> 2) doc: at the class level, in the documentation
>

The CVODE implementation is a drop-in replacement, so I kept the
available documentation. I can surely add more documentation wherever
needed.

> 3) evaluations: how do the different solvers (within and outside of
> CVODE) compare. Does it actually do a reasonable job with a stiff
> solver on a non-stiff problem? Should we be looking at ARKode or LSODA
> instead?
>
>

The underlying algorithms in CVODE are the same as LSODA ((BDF and
Adams-Moulton). I haven't looked at the LSODA implementation, but I
suspect that it might have some small numerical differences. An
interesting aspect of LSODA is that it has heuristics builtin to switch
automatically between the explicit and implicit methods. Comparisons are
great, but I fear the results might be too problem-specific to
generalize. I would maybe even advocate the ability for the user to
decide on the method used (as well as absolute and relative tolerances!
). Using the simulation mode in stan, the user can investigate which
method gives the best trade-off.
Tom

estimate.

>
>

The underlying algorithms in CVODE are the same as LSODA ((BDF and
Adams-Moulton). I haven't looked at the LSODA implementation, but I
suspect that it might have some small numerical differences. An
interesting aspect of LSODA is that it has heuristics builtin to switch
automatically between the explicit and implicit methods. Comparisons are
great, but I fear the results might be too problem-specific to
generalize. I would maybe even advocate the ability for the user to
decide on the method used (as well as absolute and relative tolerances!

method gives the best trade-off.

Thanks for the info. I didn't realize it was using a heuristic to go between the two.

Hi!

I got the code up and running on a fairly large example:

- Installation went semi-smoothly due to the yet experimental state of things, but install-cvode worked (after a cmake install)

- My model compiled with the develop cmdstan

- It starts to run and things look promising

Looking forward to the progress here, I really hope this gets ODEs going faster.

Cheers,
Sebastian

parts:
> On May 30, 2015, at 12:56 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Concerning speed: What confused me is that you, Tom, suggest smaller tolerances which I would expect to make things slower, no?

Tom used smaller tolerances. When we compare speeds,
the tolerances should be the same.

I have no idea how much these tolerances matter. We
need to experiment more.
> In any case - I agree that having these fairly crucial parameters configurable by the user is indeed important.

We can add control for tolerances as one or two more arguments
to integrate_ode. Both absolute and relative?

Stan functions don't have optional parameters, so I'm always
reluctant to add params until we're sure we'll need them.

We could also do this through the compiler if we think we
just need to find the right global setting. That is, they
wouldn't be part of a model, but part of how it's compiled:

program <- stan_model(file="foo.stan", ode_tol_absolute=1e-6, ode_tol_relative=1e-6, ...);
> Out of curiosity: To my knowledge cvode needs Jacobians as input - is the Stan autodiff used to get this?

Nope --- not Stan autodiff yet --- I believe it just uses finite diffs
internally.

Michael's worked out the math so we can supply the Jacobians
with the sensitivities --- it's going to require higher-order
autodiff, though, with multiple passes per evaluation to get the
Jacobian, so it's not necessarily going to be any faster.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
parts:
I have a model which can be a little sensitive to errors in the ODE
solution, so I made the tolerances much lower and thus slower.

The choice of the tolerances depends entirely on the model used and what
is expected from it. Like most tolerances and thresholds, it's not an
easy matter.

CVODE does require jacobians, but it has a default option to compute
them using Finite Differencing. However, in my implementation, stan's
autodiff is used to supply the jacobians to CVODE. In the sensitivities
case, you need the hessian of the ODE which I currently computed using
FD on top of autodiff. The stability needs some further investigation,
but speed-wise it is better than FD-ing a huge, very sparse matrix.

Tom

Hi Bob,

There's quite a large collection of possible arguments for CVODE, so I'm struggling to decide what to make available and what to leave as defaults. Also I'm new to CVODE having been a regular LSODA user. Based on an initial read of the CVODE docs I recommend the following as arguments in the "expert" function. I nay suggest more on further reading.

* Arguments of CVodeCreate(lmm, iter)
** lmm = linear multistep method: CV ADAMS or CV BDF
** iter = type of nonlinear solver iteration: CV NEWTON
or CV FUNCTIONAL.
** You could restrict this to the pairs (CV ADAMS, CV FUNCTIONAL) for nonstiff
problems and (CV BDF, CV NEWTON) for stiff problems.

* Linear solver used for Newton iterations: cvdense, cvband, cvklu, cvsuperlumt, cvdiag, cvspgmr, cvspbcg, or cvsptfqmr.
** I could live with the default (CVDENSE), but models involving large systems with specific matrix structures could benefit from the choice.

Cheers,
Bill

parts:
Thanks for the input. We'll probably have two calls: config-everythnig
and use-the-defaults.

We have to decide whether to make the functions in Stan solver-dependent.
Right now, it's just "solve_ode()" to call our non-stiff solver. But are
we going to turn that into:

solve_ode_sundials_adams(...., ...optional config params for sundials adams...)

???

- Bob

> On Jun 16, 2015, at 5:26 AM, Tom Haber <tom....@uhasselt.be> wrote:
>
> I would love to be able to switch between ADAMS and BDF in CVODE in
> addition to the maximum number of iterations allowed and maybe the
> initial step size (if you have expert knowledge about the ODE system,
> you can avoid some computations).
>
> Tom
>
> On Tue, 2015-06-02 at 12:58 -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> We haven't even decided on CVODE vs. other solvers in Sundials or
>> some reimplementation/translation of LSODA in C(++).
>>
>> The expert function would have to set all of the options provided,
>> or we'd have to invent a new syntax just for optional args to
>> ODEs --- there are no optional arguments in Stan itself as is.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>>> On Jun 2, 2015, at 9:45 AM, Bill Gillespie <bi...@metrumrg.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> Hi Bob,
>>>
>>> There's quite a large collection of possible arguments for CVODE, so I'm struggling to decide what to make available and what to leave as defaults. Also I'm new to CVODE having been a regular LSODA user. Based on an initial read of the CVODE docs I recommend the following as arguments in the "expert" function. I nay suggest more on further reading.
>>>
>>> * Arguments of CVodeCreate(lmm, iter)
>>> ** lmm = linear multistep method: CV ADAMS or CV BDF
>>> ** iter = type of nonlinear solver iteration: CV NEWTON
>>> or CV FUNCTIONAL.
>>> ** You could restrict this to the pairs (CV ADAMS, CV FUNCTIONAL) for nonstiff
>>> problems and (CV BDF, CV NEWTON) for stiff problems.

> On Jun 22, 2015, at 5:34 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> This puzzles me a bit, I hope cvode can be run in a faster way (I already went to 1e-6 absolute and relative tolerances).

I'd have only expected it to be faster if there was substantial
stiffness in the equations. Otherwise, the Boost thing's doing far
less work per iteration.

> @Tom: Any suggestions? What parameters are important to take care of (Stan wise and cvode wise)?
>
> Out of curiosity: Is it thinkable to get
>
> http://headmyshoulder.github.io/odeint-v2/doc/boost_numeric_odeint/tutorial/parallel_computation_with_openmp_and_mpi.html
>
> up and running in Stan with the good old boost odeint integrator?

> The instructions sound very straightforward or am I overlooking something which prevents openMP for ODE solving in Stan fundamentally? Usually I get to hear "autodiff" is the killer, but isn't this now separate enough from autodiff?

This should be possible. Our interface now just calls the ODE solver
with double values, so there's no race conditions with autodiff variables.
It may be possible to do the same with CVODE or other approaches, too.

I created a feature request and assigned it to Daniel, since this
is mostly going to be ODE and make-related (sorry, Daniel!):

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1511

We haven't been too worried about parallelism up until now because most
of our users fit modestly sized models on desktops/notebooks and have
at most four cores, which are fully occupied running four chains in
parallel. But now that we're up against bigger models, putting each chain out
to a multiprocessor makes sense if we can manage.

- Bob
